claims.text: The initial material is a solidified, equiatomic, single-phase FCC Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy.
The favorable strength–ductility balance of Co-free FeNiCrMn is caused by grain-boundary-mediated dislocation nucleation.
Grain boundaries, with efficiency dependent on their local structure and misorientation, are preferential nucleation sites for 1/6<112> partial dislocations.
Partials nucleated at grain boundaries propagate into the bulk and leave stacking faults.
The resulting stacking faults impede subsequent dislocation motion.
Interactions between stacking faults and later dislocations enhance strain hardening.
This grain-boundary and stacking-fault process delays catastrophic yielding or failure and maintains ductility.
Relative to a single crystal, bicrystals nucleate partial dislocations and develop stacking faults at lower applied strains.
Partial-dislocation nucleation and rapid stacking-fault formation coincide with a stress drop in bicrystals.
Bicrystals have lower peak stress and peak strain than corresponding single crystals because grain boundaries provide preferred dislocation-nucleation sites.
A small-twist-angle Σ111 boundary can be especially efficient at nucleating partial dislocations, whereas a coherent Σ3 boundary can instead permit homogeneous bulk nucleation.
Σ111 is an example of a high-energy boundary, while coherent Σ3 is an example of a low-energy boundary.
Elevating temperature from about 300 K to 1000 K lowers absolute stress levels under strain rates of 10^7 to 10^9 s^-1.
The elevated-temperature softening is caused by increased dislocation mobility.
Grain-boundary-assisted nucleation remains operative at elevated temperature and thereby preserves ductility.
Temperature and strain rate modulate the nucleation stress and onset of stacking-fault formation in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to the FCC solid-solution regime at approximately 300–1000 K and strain rates of 10^7–10^9 s^-1.
The controlled comparison is between single crystals and bicrystals with defined grain-boundary characters tested at identical temperature and strain rate.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in nucleation or stacking-fault-onset strain for high-energy-boundary specimens, or indistinguishable bicrystal and single-crystal stress–strain curves, would falsify the hypothesis.
Local chemical variations at grain boundaries may modulate the proposed mechanism.
